I've been meaning to write up a retrospective on the entire Jurassic Park series, specifically to discuss exactly what Jurassic World got right that the first two sequels missed (in 3's case, by a mile).

So, Jurassic Park. That movie had a lot going for it. Alan Grant had a strong character arc, and the supporting characters were generally very well done. John Hammond was spectacular, Ian Malcolm was funny and helped drive the movie's themes home without sounding preachy, and even the kids were tolerable. That last one is a backhanded compliment but that's kind of a problem with child actors in general, they haven't had nearly enough time to master their craft but their performance still needs to measure up in the same film as people who have decades of experience on them. The soundtrack pops so much that people who don't pay the slightest bit of attention to movie soundtracks can recognize it instantly. The CGI holds up today and was groundbreaking for its time, miles ahead of anything that anyone had seen before.

What was missing from the Lost World? It was a good movie, but it fell far short of Jurassic Park. Why? It was, for one thing, more 90s. The environmental message was stronger and accompanied by the protagonists engaging in actual acts of ecological terrorism against an evil corporation. Ian Malcolm and his all-black look and cynical wit was now the main character. This was a tone shift, but it wasn't really a bad one, and it is generally emblematic of how Lost World worked: It took Jurassic Park and shifted it into new environments, with new characters, and a new plot. Only a small thread of continuity was left to the first movie, and Alan Grant and Ellie Sattler are nowhere to be seen. And this was a very wise move. Especially in 1997 when Jurassic Park was still not too far from anyone's mind, taking the main attraction (dinosaurs!) and basic themes (you can't control nature!) that were at the heart of the original and then changing almost everything else - the setting to a wild island and then a city rather than a functioning theme park about to debut, switching out the cast almost completely and in particular removing the main character who already had a complete arc - was and is exactly what a sequel should do.

Which doesn't answer our question. If Lost World was doing it right when they shifted tone, what were they doing wrong? They were impatient. Jurassic Park has an initial scene with a dinosaur attack to set the stakes, but this was followed by a long buildup before we see another dino attack. We introduce Grant, Sattler, and Hammond, we introduce Ian Malcolm, we see a herd of sauropods, the scientists and lawyer who've been introduced debate their endorsement of the park over lunch, we introduce Lex and Tim, Grant, Sattler, and Malcolm discuss the diet of a triceratops while Nedry sets up his eventual betrayal and we are now sixty three minutes into our two hour film and now the tyrannosaurus is finally tearing the deactivated electric fence up and menacing the cars. Jurassic Park held audience attention early on with the awesome size and beauty of the dinosaurs.

Now, Lost World was never going to have an easy time of doing this. Jurassic Park had been out for four years, people knew that movies could have photorealistic sauropods in them. It also didn't have nearly as much setup to worry about. They didn't have to explain the safeguards of the park so they could later explain how they failed. They didn't have to explain the genetics of the dinosaurs so they could later explain how life found a way around them. They didn't have to explain how they got dinosaurs here in the modern day in the first place. The audience already knows how Jurassic Park works, and most of the movie's exposition happens in the first five minutes while Ian Malcolm talks to John Hammond. Hammond says there was a second island with more dinosaurs, the safeguards went offline in a hurricane, now the dinosaurs are free, please go observe them to boost public interest in preserving these dinosaurs so my evil nephew doesn't take over the company, boom, exposition over. The first time we see a genuine action scene (after the opening scene, following the pattern of the first film) is only thirty five minutes in, when the evil corporation hunts down and tranqs some dinos, including a pachycephalosaurus ramming a guy through a car. It's at forty-five minutes when we see a triceratops unleashed from its cage to rampage through camp. Lost World is two minutes longer, so it's not like the shorter buildup is proportional to a shorter runtime.

By dispensing with half of the buildup, when the dinosaurs do start chasing the people down it doesn't feel nearly as much like an attack sprung on an otherwise peaceful area. Instead, it feels a bit more like characters are action heroes who waded into danger. This is hardly unintentional: Ian Malcolm is extremely aware that there's a high risk of danger and no one else knows what they're dealing with. Rather than reprising his role as the only man with insight throughout the entire sixty minute buildup, the Lost World establishes a sense of danger and risk thirty minutes in with the arrival of human opposition. Ian's vindication doesn't really come for another half-hour when the T-rexes attack the trailer while Sarah Harding tries to heal the infant rex, the first time dinosaurs successfully menace our heroes, but long after the film's human antagonists got a chance to raise the stakes with an action scene. The two films have a pretty similar runtime between the moment when the movie begins and the moment the protagonists are left stranded half an island away from safety with lots of dinosaurs running wild in between, but in Lost World that situation isn't a payoff to an hour of establishing characters and safety within the confines of a perfectly safe nature walk in which Ian Malcolm is the only one who's bothered and everyone else is fine and, even if they agree with Ian philosophically, fully expect to walk away from this with all their limbs intact. The Lost World's far more action-centered plot also comes in the way the dinosaurs are treated. No longer an unstoppable force of nature who can only be escaped once unleashed, the dinosaurs including a rex are successfully captured multiple times, including once by the protagonists and a velociraptor is impaled by one of the protagonists. While the scene in general and Ian's line immediately after are really good, they demonstrate a shift in philosophy between the two movies: In Jurassic Park, you were awed by the beauty of the dinosaurs and then confronted by how uncontrollably dangerous they are. In Lost World, you are immediately confronted by their danger and then confronted by steadily more danger as time goes on. The loss of control is actually induced by the protagonists throughout the entire first half of the movie, in that they are directly responsible for the destruction of Roland Tembo's camp and indirectly cause the destruction of their own mobile HQ. Whereas in the first film Nedry causes the loss of control but then loses control himself due to a combination of a hurricane and an opportunistic dilophasaur, in the second film the protagonists intentionally try to disrupt control, succeed, and as a result one of them is eaten and the rest must flee across the island. Good job? The movie is at its best at the very end, when it is again a corporation trying to control the rex and failing, resulting in the San Diego rampage.

This thematic shift is what really harms Lost World, even though it is still a pretty good film on its own - Ian Malcolm is still a good character and the dinosaur chase scenes remain tense and well-built on their own, they just lose a bit of punch from a lack of contrasting safety in the first half of the movie.

The sins of Jurassic Park III are much easier to expound upon as compared to the Lost World, because Jurassic Park III was very bad in some very obvious ways. They brought back Alan Grant, even though he already had a completed character arc. His new character arc was about getting over the trauma of the first movie, which he accomplished by again getting chased across an island by dinosaurs and seeing multiple people around him killed. This is like Ian Malcolm's Lost World arc, except stupid. The setting is Isla Sorna, again. The plot is the same as Lost World with the San Diego scene chopped off: Go to island, means of escape destroyed, flee across island to find new means of escape. Everything, everything is lifted from an earlier Jurassic Park movie and given only very slight tweaks. Except for the series mascot, which they have quickly slaughtered to be replaced by something that is functionally identical, wasting the audience buy-in to the threat of the tyrannosaurus to try and wow audiences with something that's even bigger. Jurassic Park III can't do anything but copy its predecessors in the areas that really matter - plot, setting, character arcs - but when it comes time to honor the symbols and themes that tie the series together, it is blatantly disrespectful in discarding them to try and make its own stamp on things, an ambition you might be able to respect if this film had a shred of originality to justify its arrogance. And the appearance of the spinosaurus dino (which Alan Grant can somehow tell is bigger based on its roar - that extra ten percent body length apparently shifts you from baritone to bass)? Twenty minutes in. Lost World lacked Jurassic Park's exceptional patience, but Jurassic Park III has no patience at all. They can barely wait to get the premise established so they can fling their new dino at you.
